p\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOur use of data and statistics has been ever-growing within the articles that we write at \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe Athletic\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, drawing upon different metrics to highlight strengths, weaknesses, or patterns observed in a certain team or player.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSome of these analytics metrics will be very familiar to you by now, while others might need a little bit more explanation. Much like the \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1997663/2020/10/29/nfl-analytics-glossary-dvoa-epa-qbr/\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eNFL analytics glossary\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e from \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe Athletic\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, this is our attempt at explaining some of the most common football metrics and how to use them. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSo let’s dive in\u0026#8230;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e1. \u0026#8220;Per 90\u0026#8221; metrics\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is an important place to start when outlining metrics in football analytics, at a player and a team level. Using raw, total numbers for a metric can be misleading, as it does not account for the minutes played to reach that number. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eContext is key, and we need to find a fair way to compare performance by looking at those numbers within the context of a full game (per 90 minutes or \u0026#8220;per 90\u0026#8221;).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSince the start of the 2019-20 season, Liverpool’s Sadio Mane has scored 29 goals in the Premier League, while Tammy Abraham has only scored 21 for Chelsea.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis would initially point to Mane being the more clinical player in front of goal, but the added context is that Mane has played more than 2,000 minutes more than Abraham in this period. When you look at this goal output per 90, we see Abraham actually scores at a higher rate (0.58 goals per 90) than Mane (0.47 goals per 90) — which makes more sense given their different roles across the forward line.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA closer look at the top goalscorers from the 2020-21 season is interesting to see on a per 90 basis. Considering only players who have played 900-plus minutes in the Premier League, the player with the highest goal rate was Tottenham Hotspur loanee \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/gareth-bale-diIWb0te3Y5o4AsA/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eGareth Bale\u003c/a\u003e. While he may not have accrued as many minutes as some of his peers, \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eBale’s rate of more than one goal per 90 minutes is an outstanding return for the time he was on the pitch.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730807 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1228\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1-278x300.png 278w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1-947x1024.png 947w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e2. Expected goals (xG)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA lot of the football world will have at least heard of xG by now. Put simply, xG is a way to measure the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eNot all shots are equal in their quality — one shot might be a speculative 40-yarder and another might be a two-yard tap-in. Therefore, xG measures the quality of each shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ebefore the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, taking into account many factors, including:\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe shot angle \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe distance from goal\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether it was with the head, or with the weaker/stronger foot\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether it was from a cross, through ball, short pass etc\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether there were multiple defenders in the way\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIt is important to note that different data providers have slight differences in the factors they consider to go into their xG model. Nevertheless, the xG value is always presented as a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). For example, this shot below taken by Bruno Fernandes vs Southampton had an xG value of 0.3, which means that the\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003e shot would be \u003cb\u003e\u003ci\u003eexpected\u003c/i\u003e\u003c/b\u003e to be a \u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003ci\u003egoal\u003c/i\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e 3 times out of 10 (or 30 times out of 100), given the situation he found himself in. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"aligncenter wp-image-2730828 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-scaled.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"2560\" height=\"1443\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-scaled.jpg 2560w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-300x169.jpg 300w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-1024x577.jpg 1024w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-1536x866.jpg 1536w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-2048x1155.jpg 2048w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2560px) 100vw, 2560px\" /\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe xG value is calculated using thousands of previous shots that were similar to that situation, and seeing how many of those were scored as a result. Importantly, the value does not consider the \u003ci data-stringify-type=\"italic\"\u003equality\u003c/i\u003e of the player shooting, but instead provides a value based on how the “average” player would perform in a similar situation. Therefore, the quality of a player’s shot execution might significantly improve that chance — which we will come onto next.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe examples above use xG on a single shot to outline the metric itself, but it is often not too insightful to explore xG on a shot-by-shot basis. What we can do is add up a player or team’s xG throughout a game, period, or season to give a clearer idea of how many goals they should have scored, based on the quality of shots they had. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOf course, it is more reliable to draw insight from such information when you have a larger sample to work from, across a longer period of time. When we do this, we can use xG to explore whether a certain player or team is under or over-performing in front of goal compared with their expectation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e3. Expected goals on target (xGOT)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eBuilding on xG, we can dig deeper into the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal. Whereas xG provides a value of the shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ebefore the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, expected goals on target (xGOT) provides a modified value of an on-target shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eafter the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe value presented is the same — a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). But it adds further context by crediting the shots that head towards the top corner vs those that are straight down the middle of the goal. As you would imagine, this xGOT model only calculates a value for shots that are on target, so relies on the player to at least work the keeper to be registered — of course, if the shot is off-target your chance of scoring a goal is zero (barring an unlikely deflection). \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLet’s take this example below from Harry Kane last season. Before he takes the shot outside the area, his xG is 0.03 — a low-value chance that would be expected to be a goal only three times out of 100. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"aligncenter wp-image-2730776 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"720\" height=\"400\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1.png 720w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1-300x167.png 300w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px\" /\u003e\u003cspan\u003eHowever, the quality of the strike from Kane is outstanding, as it flies into the top corner. Having taken the shot, the xGOT value of this chance now jumps up to 0.54, meaning that the location of that strike would lead to a goal 54 per cent of the time. A high-quality finish indeed.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"wp-image-2730778 size-full aligncenter\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"720\" height=\"400\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2.png 720w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2-300x167.png 300w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px\" /\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe main thing xGOT provides is a clearer idea of a player’s shot execution. If a player has an xGOT value that is consistently higher than their xG, this tells us that they are shooting at a better rate than the quality of the chances they are getting.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIt is worth noting that such figures do only include shots that hit the target, which unfortunately excludes blocked shots. Therefore, there may be some players who can count themselves unlucky that they executed the perfect shot but the defender simply got in the way.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can then use Opta\u0026#8217;s metric of \u0026#8220;shooting goals added\u0026#8221; which calculates the difference between a player\u0026#8217;s xG and xGOT. Below, you can see that Tottenham Hotspur’s Son Heung-min added the most value to his shots last season, by improving his chances of scoring by 3.8 goals from the placement of those shots.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733204 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1120\" height=\"1290\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2.png 1120w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2-260x300.png 260w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2-889x1024.png 889w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1120px) 100vw, 1120px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eAt the other end of the scale, it was \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"678\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/leicester-city/\"\u003eLeicester City\u003c/a\u003e\u0026#8217;s Jamie Vardy with the biggest discrepancy between the chances he found himself in vs his execution of those chances, underperforming by 3.4 goals owing to poor technique in placing his on-target efforts on goal.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733206 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1120\" height=\"1290\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1.png 1120w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1-260x300.png 260w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1-889x1024.png 889w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1120px) 100vw, 1120px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLikewise, we can look at xGOT as a good way to measure goalkeeper performance. This provides a more accurate reflection of performance as it shows how many goals a goalkeeper is \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eexpected\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e to have conceded based on the quality of the shots on target they have faced.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can then use this to measure the number of “goals prevented” — this compares how many goals a goalkeeper actually conceded against the number they were expected to. The higher the goals prevented number, the better the shot-stopping performance.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLast season, the best shot-stopping performance was from Hugo Lloris at Tottenham Hotspur, who kept out 5.1 goals above expectation across the season. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730831 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1280\" height=\"2522\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented.png 1280w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-152x300.png 152w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-520x1024.png 520w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-780x1536.png 780w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-1039x2048.png 1039w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1280px) 100vw, 1280px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e4. Non-penalty goals\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis metric requires little explanation, but it is important to consider why goalscoring tallies are often assessed by removing penalty goals from the total. Penalties themselves are not a great indicator of a player’s ability to generate chances for themselves. Of course, \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2139959/2020/10/17/penalty-golden-boot-les-ferdinand/\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eyou can have a player who both wins and takes penalties\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, but often the penalty taker is handed the ball even if they were not involved in the play leading up to the foul. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eChanges to handball rules, and the microscopic scrutiny from the introduction of VAR also means that the number of penalties awarded was at an all-time high last season with 125 spot-kicks in total — an average of one penalty every three games.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePenalty takers can inflate their numbers quite significantly from what is ultimately an unsustainable source of goalscoring income. Looking at last season’s top goalscorers in the Premier League, Manchester United’s Fernandes and Leicester City’s Vardy both doubled their goal tally from the spot and would be far from the top 10 goalscorers without such high-value opportunities to score (approximately 0.75 xG for those interested).\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2732927 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\" /\u003e\u003cspan\u003eGiven this, it is a little more reliable to assess goalscoring opportunities in open play by looking at non-penalty goals or non-penalty xG — where you provide more of a level playing field to explore a team or player’s opportunity to score.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e5. Expected assists (xA)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAssists themselves can be a very poor indication of a player’s creative ability. One player could play a simple two-yard pass for their team-mate to put one in the top corner, while another could run the length of the field and put it on a plate for their team-mate to score. Hardly comparable. Also, to register an assist, the passer is reliant on the receiver to finish the chance — which does not always happen.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTherefore, another extension of the expected goals framework is expected assists (xA). It works in much the same way as xG, but works back slightly in giving credit to the player who passed the ball before the shot was taken.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePut simply, xA measures the expected goals value of the shot that is assisted, and is also presented as a number between zero (no chance of an assist) and one (a certain assist). \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used:\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e xA can provide credit to those creative players and gives a clearer idea of how many assists a player \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eshould\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e have, given the quality of their attacking output. We can similarly add up all of the values to explore whether a player is creating highly valuable chances or playing it a little more safe in their passing.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eLooking at last season, it is no surprise to see \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"654\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/manchester-city/\"\u003eManchester City\u003c/a\u003e talisman \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"TX7pFeb0aiHzuvjI\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/kevin-de-bruyne-TX7pFeb0aiHzuvjI/\"\u003eKevin De Bruyne\u003c/a\u003e lead the way for the most creative player. Given that the Belgian missed a fair share of games through injury, looking on a \u0026#8220;per 90\u0026#8221; basis once again highlights his quality when he is in the team — providing passes worthy of an assist at a rate of more than one every three games (0.37 xA per 90).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730839 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1252\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists-272x300.png 272w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists-929x1024.png 929w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eOf course, just as penalties can inflate a player\u0026#8217;s goal output, being a set-piece taker (i.e. corners or free-kicks) can also inflate a player\u0026#8217;s creative output, given that they have a greater opportunity to deliver the ball, unopposed, into a dangerous area with more players to attack the ball. Therefore, it is worth looking at last season\u0026#8217;s xA among all players in open play, which shows a slightly different configuration. Here, Fernandes just about claims top spot ahead of De Bruyne, while players like \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"00OFm841hooAS8V3\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/callum-hudson-odoi-00OFm841hooAS8V3/\"\u003eCallum Hudson-Odoi\u003c/a\u003e and Allan Saint-Maximin show their creative quality to find team-mates in dangerous positions with their passing in open play.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733134 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1252\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP-272x300.png 272w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP-929x1024.png 929w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\" /\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e6. Passes per defensive action (PPDA)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePasses per defensive action (PPDA) is a proxy of pressing intensity at the team level, used to try and capture the degree to which an opponent is pressuring the opposition when they don’t have the ball. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003ePut simply, this metric counts how many passes a team allows the opposition to make before attempting to win the ball back with a defensive action, such as a tackle, interception, or clearance. Importantly, this metric applies only to a certain area of the pitch — the final 60 per cent of the pitch to be precise — roughly in line with the edge of the centre circle in your own half.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA low PPDA number indicates \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ehigher\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e intensity when trying to win the ball back and a higher figure indicates a team that is more passive without the ball. As you can see below, Marcelo Bielsa’s Leeds were unsurprisingly the most intense off the ball with an average PPDA of 9.3 last season, while Newcastle United were nearly half as intense in their pressing with a PPDA of 18.3 as they preferred to drop back into shape when losing possession.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733096 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eJust as above, PPDA can give an indication of a team’s intent to win the ball back. It can show which teams are more active in trying to regain possession when they lose it. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eImportantly, PPDA doesn’t give us any indication of the \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003esuccess\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e of that strategy — it is more indicative of a team’s \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003estyle\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e in winning the ball back. As teams such as Liverpool and Manchester City have shown in recent years, pressing is most effective when the team acts in unison and knows when to pounce. Which can bring us nicely onto our next term…\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e7. Pressures\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis metric is a little more \u0026#8220;what is says on the tin\u0026#8221;, but it’s important to know why it is useful. Here, we turn to StatsBomb who provide this data, and define pressures as the “number of times applying pressure to the opposing player who is receiving, carrying or releasing the ball”. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis can be studied at player or team level to show the intent in pressing the ball, rather than simply the outcome of making a tackle or block. The higher the number of pressures, the more the player or team attempted to engage with the opponent on the ball. Be careful here though, as more pressures may not mean a higher intensity per se, but might just mean that the team had less possession of the ball. We can account for this by adjusting the metric for the amount of possession — something we will come onto below.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eUsing this information, we can consider how often that pressure was successful — i.e. the quality of the press that leads to a turnover of possession. StatsBomb pressure data via \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://fbref.com/en/squads/361ca564/2020-2021/matchlogs/s10728/defense/Tottenham-Hotspur-Match-Logs-Premier-League\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003efbref\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e provides this with “successful pressure percentage”, defined as the percentage of time that a team gained possession within five seconds of applying the pressure.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAs you can see below, champions Manchester City were the most co-ordinated in their press, regaining possession 32 per cent of the time when making their pressures. Meanwhile, Newcastle United remained rooted to the bottom of the table once again, alongside relegation sufferers Sheffield United with a pressure success of 25 per cent. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733094 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eUnfortunately, there is not a silver bullet metric for measuring pressing among teams, but using the PPDA metric alongside this pressure data can be useful to build a picture of a team\u0026#8217;s style to win the ball back and understand how successful they are when they do look to regain possession.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e8. Possession-adjusted metrics\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen considering defensive metrics (e.g. tackles, blocks, interceptions), a player’s ability is not represented reliably by the raw numbers. \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1692489/2020/03/23/the-10-commandments-of-football-analytics/\"\u003eA busy defender isn’t always a good one\u003c/a\u003e, and many defensive metrics most often represent a team or player’s \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003estyle\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e rather than their quality.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOne way we can help to overcome this issue is to \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eadjust\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e these defensive metrics based on the amount of possession a team has. Why do we do this? Essentially, a player can only perform a defensive action when their team does \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003enot\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e have the ball. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIf a team has less possession of the ball, they have more \u003cem\u003eopportunities\u003c/em\u003e to defend. Therefore, it is difficult to reliably compare the defensive contribution between, for example, Manchester City vs Newcastle United based on the raw frequency of defensive actions (e.g. blocks per 90 minutes).\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhat we can do is adjust these defensive statistics for the number of times that they make these actions for every 1,000 opponent touches — which allows us to assess all players on more of a level playing field.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLet’s run through an example. Manchester City full-back Joao Cancelo\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eaverages 2.4 interceptions per 90, which was enough to rank him 16th among all defenders in the Premier League last season. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen adjusting for possession, he jumps to 4.2 interceptions per 1,000 opponent touches, which ranks him 9th among the group of defenders. This accounts for the fact that Manchester City were so dominant in possession, so gives more credit to Cancelo’s actions when City don’t have the ball.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is definitely one to look out for when you next see a players’ defensive statistics — more actions does not necessarily mean a better defender.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e9. Field tilt\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eField tilt is a simple way of showing the territorial dominance between teams. Put simply, it measures the share of possession a team has in a game, considering only touches or passes in the attacking third.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSo, if Team A makes a total of 80 final-third passes, and Team B attempts just 20 final-third passes, Team A has a field tilt of 80 per cent. The better attacking teams usually dominate this metric because they have more of the ball in attacking areas. As you can see below, Manchester City and Liverpool, in particular, were suffocating teams by keeping possession in the attacking third last season.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733184 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\" /\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eField tilt is useful in revealing which side is more dominant in matches. Rather than simply looking at the average possession statistics, field tilt provides a clearer picture of where that possession is. It’s not always about simply keeping the ball, it’s about getting into the areas that matter.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLikewise, it can be an interesting way to explore the change in a team’s dominance in the final third, over time. For example, in the 2019-20 season, Aston Villa had a field tilt of 41 per cent, meaning the opposition had more passes in their final third than Villa did in the opponent’s final third. It also ranked Villa as 18th in the Premier League for such territorial dominance that season.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn contrast, Villa had a field tilt of 50 per cent in the 2020-21 season which was the ninth-best in the league. They were having a larger share of the play in the opposition\u0026#8217;s final third than they did in the previous season, getting the ball into greater areas of threat for longer.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn isolation, field tilt metrics may not provide too much insight towards a team’s success, but it does give an indication of their style in getting the ball into advanced areas compared with the opposition. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e10. Game state\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAnother straightforward term, but one that can provide crucial context when evaluating a team’s metrics.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eGame state refers to whether the team is in a losing, drawing or winning position when they are performing certain actions. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is important to consider, as it can heavily influence a team’s approach during the game. A team that is losing is more likely to chase the game by taking more shots and creating more chances. By contrast, a team that is winning might be more likely to defend a lead and subsequently create fewer chances because of the game state they find themselves in.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAs outlined above, the main use of this is to provide further context as to why a team may have certain performance metrics. For example, Tottenham Hotspur didn’t attempt a single shot in the second half at home to Arsenal last season. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eInstantly, this suggests weak attacking play from Spurs, but they had built a 2-0 lead before half-time. Therefore, the game state meant Spurs were in a winning position, so their low attacking output was contextualised by them protecting their lead.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eLooking at the game state across the season for each team, we can see that \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"656\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/tottenham-hotspur/\"\u003eSpurs\u003c/a\u003e actually spent a long time in a winning position compared with others in the league, something which is likely to have fuelled the frustration towards the recently-departed Jose Mourinho, as Spurs often retreated after taking the lead.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"wp-image-2733696 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-scaled.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"2560\" height=\"1891\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-scaled.jpg 2560w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-300x222.jpg 300w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-1024x756.jpg 1024w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-1536x1135.jpg 1536w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27120741/PL-20-21-2048x1513.jpg 2048w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2560px) 100vw, 2560px\" /\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eMeanwhile, many may point to champions Manchester City having the lowest goals scored in a season since Pep Guardiola arrived (83 goals), but the added context is that they spent more than half their time in the lead — more than any other team in the league — and were not obliged to score any additional goals to pick up three points.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eGame state can determine the tactical approach taken by a team, and provides useful context when assessing both attacking and defensive metrics at the player or team level.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr /\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e11.  Sequences and possessions\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003eThis could be a whole article on its own, but the principle of sequences and possessions is very simple.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA sequence starts with a player making a controlled action on the ball — i.e. making a pass is controlled but making a tackle is not controlled. Opta defines a sequence as a \u0026#8220;passage of play which belongs to one team and are ended by defensive actions, stoppages in play or a shot\u0026#8221;.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eFor example, if a team makes 15 passes and works it forward before the opposition defender clears it out for a throw-in, that would be one sequence. When the player throws it back in to a team-mate, that starts a second sequence but importantly, the team still has possession of the ball.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eTherefore, possessions are the combination of one or more sequences in a row belonging to the same team. That possession continues until the opposition wins the ball back by making a controlled action on the ball themselves — thus starting their own sequence of play.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThink of it like a chain — the sequences are the individual links which join together to make the overall chain (i.e. possession).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003eThese metrics help us to build a wider picture of a team or player, beyond simple event metrics (i.e. a pass). It can help to show the style of a team in how many passes they tend to have within a sequence — i.e. Manchester City tend to have more passes within a sequence of play than \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"675\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/burnley/\"\u003eBurnley\u003c/a\u003e do.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eBy looking at the number of possessions between the teams, we can understand \u003ca href=\"https://theathletic.com/1981340/2020/08/08/fernandes-manchester-united-de-bruyne-manchester-city-ball-retention-analytics/?article_source=search\u0026amp;search_query=possession\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003ethe style and tempo of games\u003c/a\u003e. Essentially, we can look at how many times the ball changed hands between the teams during the game (i.e. Team A has it until Team B has it, which continues until Team A wins it back, etc). This can help show the approach taken in games, with more possessions indicative of a higher tempo and a more frenetic game.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThere are many more avenues to take this information, but it shows the value of adding further context to understand what is occurring on the pitch based on individual events.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp style=\"text-align: right;\"\u003e\u003cem\u003e(Design: Sam Richardson)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n","article_body_desktop":"\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOur use of data and statistics has been ever-growing within the articles that we write at \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe Athletic\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, drawing upon different metrics to highlight strengths, weaknesses, or patterns observed in a certain team or player.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSome of these analytics metrics will be very familiar to you by now, while others might need a little bit more explanation. Much like the \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1997663/2020/10/29/nfl-analytics-glossary-dvoa-epa-qbr/\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eNFL analytics glossary\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e from \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe Athletic\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, this is our attempt at explaining some of the most common football metrics and how to use them.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSo let’s dive in…\u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e1. “Per 90” metrics\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is an important place to start when outlining metrics in football analytics, at a player and a team level. Using raw, total numbers for a metric can be misleading, as it does not account for the minutes played to reach that number.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eContext is key, and we need to find a fair way to compare performance by looking at those numbers within the context of a full game (per 90 minutes or “per 90”).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-container\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-wrapper\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=ad-slug-container\u003e\u003cp class=\"ad-slug\"\u003eAdvertisement\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv id=\"mid1\" data-position=\"mid1\" class=\"ad place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSince the start of the 2019-20 season, Liverpool’s Sadio Mane has scored 29 goals in the Premier League, while Tammy Abraham has only scored 21 for Chelsea.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis would initially point to Mane being the more clinical player in front of goal, but the added context is that Mane has played more than 2,000 minutes more than Abraham in this period. When you look at this goal output per 90, we see Abraham actually scores at a higher rate (0.58 goals per 90) than Mane (0.47 goals per 90) — which makes more sense given their different roles across the forward line.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA closer look at the top goalscorers from the 2020-21 season is interesting to see on a per 90 basis. Considering only players who have played 900-plus minutes in the Premier League, the player with the highest goal rate was Tottenham Hotspur loanee \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/gareth-bale-diIWb0te3Y5o4AsA/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eGareth Bale\u003c/a\u003e. While he may not have accrued as many minutes as some of his peers,\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBale’s rate of more than one goal per 90 minutes is an outstanding return for the time he was on the pitch.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730807 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1228\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1-278x300.png 278w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113054/PL-gls-per-90-1-947x1024.png 947w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e2. Expected goals (xG)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA lot of the football world will have at least heard of xG by now. Put simply, xG is a way to measure the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eNot all shots are equal in their quality — one shot might be a speculative 40-yarder and another might be a two-yard tap-in. Therefore, xG measures the quality of each shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ebefore the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, taking into account many factors, including:\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe shot angle\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe distance from goal\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether it was with the head, or with the weaker/stronger foot\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether it was from a cross, through ball, short pass etc\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli style=\"font-weight: 400;\" aria-level=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhether there were multiple defenders in the way\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIt is important to note that different data providers have slight differences in the factors they consider to go into their xG model. Nevertheless, the xG value is always presented as a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). For example, this shot below taken by Bruno Fernandes vs Southampton had an xG value of 0.3, which means that the\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003e shot would be \u003cb\u003e\u003ci\u003eexpected\u003c/i\u003e\u003c/b\u003e to be a \u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003ci\u003egoal\u003c/i\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e 3 times out of 10 (or 30 times out of 100), given the situation he found himself in.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"aligncenter wp-image-2730828 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-scaled.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"2560\" height=\"1443\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-scaled.jpg 2560w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-300x169.jpg 300w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-1024x577.jpg 1024w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-1536x866.jpg 1536w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113548/Fernandes_xG_ann-2048x1155.jpg 2048w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2560px) 100vw, 2560px\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe xG value is calculated using thousands of previous shots that were similar to that situation, and seeing how many of those were scored as a result. Importantly, the value does not consider the\u0026nbsp;\u003ci data-stringify-type=\"italic\"\u003equality\u003c/i\u003e\u0026nbsp;of the player shooting, but instead provides a value based on how the “average” player would perform in a similar situation. Therefore, the quality of a player’s shot execution might significantly improve that chance — which we will come onto next.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-container\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-wrapper\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=ad-slug-container\u003e\u003cp class=\"ad-slug\"\u003eAdvertisement\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv id=\"mid2\" data-position=\"mid2\" class=\"ad place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe examples above use xG on a single shot to outline the metric itself, but it is often not too insightful to explore xG on a shot-by-shot basis. What we can do is add up a player or team’s xG throughout a game, period, or season to give a clearer idea of how many goals they should have scored, based on the quality of shots they had.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOf course, it is more reliable to draw insight from such information when you have a larger sample to work from, across a longer period of time. When we do this, we can use xG to explore whether a certain player or team is under or over-performing in front of goal compared with their expectation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e3. Expected goals on target (xGOT)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eBuilding on xG, we can dig deeper into the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal. Whereas xG provides a value of the shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ebefore the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, expected goals on target (xGOT) provides a modified value of an on-target shot \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eafter the player shoots\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe value presented is the same — a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). But it adds further context by crediting the shots that head towards the top corner vs those that are straight down the middle of the goal. As you would imagine, this xGOT model only calculates a value for shots that are on target, so relies on the player to at least work the keeper to be registered — of course, if the shot is off-target your chance of scoring a goal is zero (barring an unlikely deflection).\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLet’s take this example below from Harry Kane last season. Before he takes the shot outside the area, his xG is 0.03 — a low-value chance that would be expected to be a goal only three times out of 100.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"aligncenter wp-image-2730776 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"720\" height=\"400\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1.png 720w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112244/Kane_xGOT_1-300x167.png 300w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eHowever, the quality of the strike from Kane is outstanding, as it flies into the top corner. Having taken the shot, the xGOT value of this chance now jumps up to 0.54, meaning that the location of that strike would lead to a goal 54 per cent of the time. A high-quality finish indeed.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"wp-image-2730778 size-full aligncenter\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"720\" height=\"400\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2.png 720w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26112252/Kane_xGOT_2-300x167.png 300w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 720px) 100vw, 720px\"\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe main thing xGOT provides is a clearer idea of a player’s shot execution. If a player has an xGOT value that is consistently higher than their xG, this tells us that they are shooting at a better rate than the quality of the chances they are getting.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIt is worth noting that such figures do only include shots that hit the target, which unfortunately excludes blocked shots. Therefore, there may be some players who can count themselves unlucky that they executed the perfect shot but the defender simply got in the way.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can then use Opta’s metric of “shooting goals added” which calculates the difference between a player’s xG and xGOT. Below, you can see that Tottenham Hotspur’s Son Heung-min added the most value to his shots last season, by improving his chances of scoring by 3.8 goals from the placement of those shots.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733204 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1120\" height=\"1290\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2.png 1120w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2-260x300.png 260w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091644/shooting_above-2-889x1024.png 889w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1120px) 100vw, 1120px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt the other end of the scale, it was \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"678\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/leicester-city/\"\u003eLeicester City\u003c/a\u003e’s Jamie Vardy with the biggest discrepancy between the chances he found himself in vs his execution of those chances, underperforming by 3.4 goals owing to poor technique in placing his on-target efforts on goal.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733206 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1120\" height=\"1290\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1.png 1120w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1-260x300.png 260w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27091654/shooting_below-1-889x1024.png 889w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1120px) 100vw, 1120px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLikewise, we can look at xGOT as a good way to measure goalkeeper performance. This provides a more accurate reflection of performance as it shows how many goals a goalkeeper is \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eexpected\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e to have conceded based on the quality of the shots on target they have faced.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can then use this to measure the number of “goals prevented” — this compares how many goals a goalkeeper actually conceded against the number they were expected to. The higher the goals prevented number, the better the shot-stopping performance.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-container\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-wrapper\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=ad-slug-container\u003e\u003cp class=\"ad-slug\"\u003eAdvertisement\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv id=\"mid3\" data-position=\"mid3\" class=\"ad place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLast season, the best shot-stopping performance was from Hugo Lloris at Tottenham Hotspur, who kept out 5.1 goals above expectation across the season.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730831 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1280\" height=\"2522\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented.png 1280w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-152x300.png 152w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-520x1024.png 520w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-780x1536.png 780w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113700/pl_gls_prevented-1039x2048.png 1039w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1280px) 100vw, 1280px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e4. Non-penalty goals\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis metric requires little explanation, but it is important to consider why goalscoring tallies are often assessed by removing penalty goals from the total. Penalties themselves are not a great indicator of a player’s ability to generate chances for themselves. Of course, \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2139959/2020/10/17/penalty-golden-boot-les-ferdinand/\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eyou can have a player who both wins and takes penalties\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, but often the penalty taker is handed the ball even if they were not involved in the play leading up to the foul.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eChanges to handball rules, and the microscopic scrutiny from the introduction of VAR also means that the number of penalties awarded was at an all-time high last season with 125 spot-kicks in total — an average of one penalty every three games.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003cdiv id=\"top-league-content-root\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003cscript id=\"top-league-content-data\" type=\"application/json\"\u003e{\"endpoint\":\"https://api-prd-nyt.theathletic.com/graphql\"}\u003c/script\u003e\n    \u003cscript defer id=\"top-league-content-script\" src=\"https://graphics-cdn.theathletic.com/dir/top-league-content.js?ver=4\"\u003e\u003c/script\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePenalty takers can inflate their numbers quite significantly from what is ultimately an unsustainable source of goalscoring income. Looking at last season’s top goalscorers in the Premier League, Manchester United’s Fernandes and Leicester City’s Vardy both doubled their goal tally from the spot and would be far from the top 10 goalscorers without such high-value opportunities to score (approximately 0.75 xG for those interested).\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2732927 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27055636/PL_pen_goals-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eGiven this, it is a little more reliable to assess goalscoring opportunities in open play by looking at non-penalty goals or non-penalty xG — where you provide more of a level playing field to explore a team or player’s opportunity to score.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"article-pickem\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e5. Expected assists (xA)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAssists themselves can be a very poor indication of a player’s creative ability. One player could play a simple two-yard pass for their team-mate to put one in the top corner, while another could run the length of the field and put it on a plate for their team-mate to score. Hardly comparable. Also, to register an assist, the passer is reliant on the receiver to finish the chance — which does not always happen.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTherefore, another extension of the expected goals framework is expected assists (xA). It works in much the same way as xG, but works back slightly in giving credit to the player who passed the ball before the shot was taken.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePut simply, xA measures the expected goals value of the shot that is assisted, and is also presented as a number between zero (no chance of an assist) and one (a certain assist).\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used:\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e xA can provide credit to those creative players and gives a clearer idea of how many assists a player \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eshould\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e have, given the quality of their attacking output. We can similarly add up all of the values to explore whether a player is creating highly valuable chances or playing it a little more safe in their passing.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLooking at last season, it is no surprise to see \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"654\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/manchester-city/\"\u003eManchester City\u003c/a\u003e talisman \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"TX7pFeb0aiHzuvjI\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/kevin-de-bruyne-TX7pFeb0aiHzuvjI/\"\u003eKevin De Bruyne\u003c/a\u003e lead the way for the most creative player. Given that the Belgian missed a fair share of games through injury, looking on a “per 90” basis once again highlights his quality when he is in the team — providing passes worthy of an assist at a rate of more than one every three games (0.37 xA per 90).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2730839 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1252\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists-272x300.png 272w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/26113846/PL-expected-assists-929x1024.png 929w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOf course, just as penalties can inflate a player’s goal output, being a set-piece taker (i.e. corners or free-kicks) can also inflate a player’s creative output, given that they have a greater opportunity to deliver the ball, unopposed, into a dangerous area with more players to attack the ball. Therefore, it is worth looking at last season’s xA among all players in open play, which shows a slightly different configuration. Here, Fernandes just about claims top spot ahead of De Bruyne, while players like \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"00OFm841hooAS8V3\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/player/callum-hudson-odoi-00OFm841hooAS8V3/\"\u003eCallum Hudson-Odoi\u003c/a\u003e and Allan Saint-Maximin show their creative quality to find team-mates in dangerous positions with their passing in open play.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733134 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"1136\" height=\"1252\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP.png 1136w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP-272x300.png 272w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27084313/PL-expected-assists-OP-929x1024.png 929w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 1136px) 100vw, 1136px\"\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e6. Passes per defensive action (PPDA)\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003ePasses per defensive action (PPDA) is a proxy of pressing intensity at the team level, used to try and capture the degree to which an opponent is pressuring the opposition when they don’t have the ball.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-container\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-wrapper\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=ad-slug-container\u003e\u003cp class=\"ad-slug\"\u003eAdvertisement\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv id=\"mid4\" data-position=\"mid4\" class=\"ad place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003ePut simply, this metric counts how many passes a team allows the opposition to make before attempting to win the ball back with a defensive action, such as a tackle, interception, or clearance. Importantly, this metric applies only to a certain area of the pitch — the final 60 per cent of the pitch to be precise — roughly in line with the edge of the centre circle in your own half.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eA low PPDA number indicates \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003ehigher\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e intensity when trying to win the ball back and a higher figure indicates a team that is more passive without the ball. As you can see below, Marcelo Bielsa’s Leeds were unsurprisingly the most intense off the ball with an average PPDA of 9.3 last season, while Newcastle United were nearly half as intense in their pressing with a PPDA of 18.3 as they preferred to drop back into shape when losing possession.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733096 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082643/PPDA_bar-1-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eJust as above, PPDA can give an indication of a team’s intent to win the ball back. It can show which teams are more active in trying to regain possession when they lose it.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cspan\u003eImportantly, PPDA doesn’t give us any indication of the \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003esuccess\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e of that strategy — it is more indicative of a team’s \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003estyle\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e in winning the ball back. As teams such as Liverpool and Manchester City have shown in recent years, pressing is most effective when the team acts in unison and knows when to pounce. Which can bring us nicely onto our next term…\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e7. Pressures\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis metric is a little more “what is says on the tin”, but it’s important to know why it is useful. Here, we turn to StatsBomb who provide this data, and define pressures as the “number of times applying pressure to the opposing player who is receiving, carrying or releasing the ball”.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis can be studied at player or team level to show the intent in pressing the ball, rather than simply the outcome of making a tackle or block. The higher the number of pressures, the more the player or team attempted to engage with the opponent on the ball. Be careful here though, as more pressures may not mean a higher intensity per se, but might just mean that the team had less possession of the ball. We can account for this by adjusting the metric for the amount of possession — something we will come onto below.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used:\u0026nbsp;\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eUsing this information, we can consider how often that pressure was successful — i.e. the quality of the press that leads to a turnover of possession. StatsBomb pressure data via \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://fbref.com/en/squads/361ca564/2020-2021/matchlogs/s10728/defense/Tottenham-Hotspur-Match-Logs-Premier-League\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003efbref\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e provides this with “successful pressure percentage”, defined as the percentage of time that a team gained possession within five seconds of applying the pressure.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAs you can see below, champions Manchester City were the most co-ordinated in their press, regaining possession 32 per cent of the time when making their pressures. Meanwhile, Newcastle United remained rooted to the bottom of the table once again, alongside relegation sufferers Sheffield United with a pressure success of 25 per cent.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733094 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27082625/Pressures_bar-1-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\"\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnfortunately, there is not a silver bullet metric for measuring pressing among teams, but using the PPDA metric alongside this pressure data can be useful to build a picture of a team’s style to win the ball back and understand how successful they are when they do look to regain possession.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-container\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"ad-wrapper\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=ad-slug-container\u003e\u003cp class=\"ad-slug\"\u003eAdvertisement\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv id=\"mid5\" data-position=\"mid5\" class=\"ad place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e8. Possession-adjusted metrics\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen considering defensive metrics (e.g. tackles, blocks, interceptions), a player’s ability is not represented reliably by the raw numbers. \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1692489/2020/03/23/the-10-commandments-of-football-analytics/\"\u003eA busy defender isn’t always a good one\u003c/a\u003e, and many defensive metrics most often represent a team or player’s \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003estyle\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e rather than their quality.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eOne way we can help to overcome this issue is to \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003eadjust\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e these defensive metrics based on the amount of possession a team has. Why do we do this? Essentially, a player can only perform a defensive action when their team does \u003c/span\u003e\u003ci\u003e\u003cspan\u003enot\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/i\u003e\u003cspan\u003e have the ball.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIf a team has less possession of the ball, they have more \u003cem\u003eopportunities\u003c/em\u003e to defend. Therefore, it is difficult to reliably compare the defensive contribution between, for example, Manchester City vs Newcastle United based on the raw frequency of defensive actions (e.g. blocks per 90 minutes).\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhat we can do is adjust these defensive statistics for the number of times that they make these actions for every 1,000 opponent touches — which allows us to assess all players on more of a level playing field.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLet’s run through an example. Manchester City full-back Joao Cancelo\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eaverages 2.4 interceptions per 90, which was enough to rank him 16th among all defenders in the Premier League last season.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen adjusting for possession, he jumps to 4.2 interceptions per 1,000 opponent touches, which ranks him 9th among the group of defenders. This accounts for the fact that Manchester City were so dominant in possession, so gives more credit to Cancelo’s actions when City don’t have the ball.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is definitely one to look out for when you next see a players’ defensive statistics — more actions does not necessarily mean a better defender.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e9. Field tilt\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eField tilt is a simple way of showing the territorial dominance between teams. Put simply, it measures the share of possession a team has in a game, considering only touches or passes in the attacking third.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSo, if Team A makes a total of 80 final-third passes, and Team B attempts just 20 final-third passes, Team A has a field tilt of 80 per cent. The better attacking teams usually dominate this metric because they have more of the ball in attacking areas. As you can see below, Manchester City and Liverpool, in particular, were suffocating teams by keeping possession in the attacking third last season.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" class=\"alignnone wp-image-2733184 size-full\" src=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt.png\" alt=\"\" width=\"2400\" height=\"3000\" srcset=\"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt.png 2400w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-240x300.png 240w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-819x1024.png 819w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-1229x1536.png 1229w, https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2021/07/27090547/field_tilt-1638x2048.png 1638w\" sizes=\"(max-width: 2400px) 100vw, 2400px\"\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eField tilt is useful in revealing which side is more dominant in matches. Rather than simply looking at the average possession statistics, field tilt provides a clearer picture of where that possession is. It’s not always about simply keeping the ball, it’s about getting into the areas that matter.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLikewise, it can be an interesting way to explore the change in a team’s dominance in the final third, over time. For example, in the 2019-20 season, Aston Villa had a field tilt of 41 per cent, meaning the opposition had more passes in their final third than Villa did in the opponent’s final third. It also ranked Villa as 18th in the Premier League for such territorial dominance that season.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn contrast, Villa had a field tilt of 50 per cent in the 2020-21 season which was the ninth-best in the league. They were having a larger share of the play in the opposition’s final third than they did in the previous season, getting the ball into greater areas of threat for longer.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn isolation, field tilt metrics may not provide too much insight towards a team’s success, but it does give an indication of their style in getting the ball into advanced areas compared with the opposition.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003e10. Game state\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAnother straightforward term, but one that can provide crucial context when evaluating a team’s metrics.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eGame state refers to whether the team is in a losing, drawing or winning position when they are performing certain actions.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThis is important to consider, as it can heavily influence a team’s approach during the game. A team that is losing is more likely to chase the game by taking more shots and creating more chances. By contrast, a team that is winning might be more likely to defend a lead and subsequently create fewer chances because of the game state they find themselves in.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAs outlined above, the main use of this is to provide further context as to why a team may have certain performance metrics. For example, Tottenham Hotspur didn’t attempt a single shot in the second half at home to Arsenal last season.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan\u003eInstantly, this suggests weak attacking play from Spurs, but they had built a 2-0 lead before half-time. Therefore, the game state meant Spurs were in a winning position, so their low attacking output was contextualised by them protecting their lead.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLooking at the game state across the season for each team, we can see that \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"656\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/tottenham-hotspur/\"\u003eSpurs\u003c/a\u003e actually spent a long time in a winning position compared with others in the league, something which is likely to have fuelled the frustration towards the recently-departed Jose Mourinho, as Spurs often retreated after taking the lead.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" place-ad\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cp\u003eGame state can determine the tactical approach taken by a team, and provides useful context when assessing both attacking and defensive metrics at the player or team level.\u003c/p\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e11.\u0026nbsp; Sequences and possessions\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eWhat it is: \u003c/b\u003eThis could be a whole article on its own, but the principle of sequences and possessions is very simple.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA sequence starts with a player making a controlled action on the ball — i.e. making a pass is controlled but making a tackle is not controlled. Opta defines a sequence as a “passage of play which belongs to one team and are ended by defensive actions, stoppages in play or a shot”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, if a team makes 15 passes and works it forward before the opposition defender clears it out for a throw-in, that would be one sequence. When the player throws it back in to a team-mate, that starts a second sequence but importantly, the team still has possession of the ball.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTherefore, possessions are the combination of one or more sequences in a row belonging to the same team. That possession continues until the opposition wins the ball back by making a controlled action on the ball themselves — thus starting their own sequence of play.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThink of it like a chain — the sequences are the individual links which join together to make the overall chain (i.e. possession).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cb\u003eHow it can be used: \u003c/b\u003eThese metrics help us to build a wider picture of a team or player, beyond simple event metrics (i.e. a pass). It can help to show the style of a team in how many passes they tend to have within a sequence — i.e. Manchester City tend to have more passes within a sequence of play than \u003ca class=\"ath_autolink\" data-id=\"675\" href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/football/team/burnley/\"\u003eBurnley\u003c/a\u003e do.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBy looking at the number of possessions between the teams, we can understand \u003ca href=\"https://theathletic.com/1981340/2020/08/08/fernandes-manchester-united-de-bruyne-manchester-city-ball-retention-analytics/?article_source=search\u0026amp;search_query=possession\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003ethe style and tempo of games\u003c/a\u003e. Essentially, we can look at how many times the ball changed hands between the teams during the game (i.e. Team A has it until Team B has it, which continues until Team A wins it back, etc). This can help show the approach taken in games, with more possessions indicative of a higher tempo and a more frenetic game.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are many more avenues to take this information, but it shows the value of adding further context to understand what is occurring on the pitch based on individual events.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp style=\"text-align: right;\"\u003e\u003cem\u003e(Design: Sam Richardson)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n","authors":[{"__typename":"ArticleAuthor","author":{"__typename":"Staff","first_name":"Mark","name":"Mark Carey","id":"6264985","avatar_uri":"https://static01.nyt.com/athletic/uploads/wp/2026/04/08104050/Testa.Mark-Carey.011-scaled.jpg","bio":"Mark Carey is a Data Analyst for The Athletic.
